extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom leaders, media observers, and readers interested in newsroom ethics and social media policy
extracted.subtask_description: A close-read analysis of a newsroom controversy focused on social media use, internal discipline, and workplace culture at a major newspaper, using a specific Washington Post episode to illustrate broader ethics and policy issues. Useful for evaluating how news organizations set and apply social-media and conduct standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and consistency of social media policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the newsroom has a clear, consistently applied social media policy; the article describes The Post's policy as 'unusual,' 'outdated,' and 'not sufficiently equitable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate if the policy gives unambiguous guidance on acceptable posts/retweets and whether enforcement has been uniform. Examples: the Post's policy led to different outcomes for staff (Sonmez barred from certain coverage in 2018; later allowed in 2021 after public protest). The union had repeatedly lobbied for updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest / impartiality standard for reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for when a reporter is disqualified from covering topics because of personal connections or public advocacy; the Post removed Sonmez from Kavanaugh coverage citing her public engagement in advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the newsroom's impartiality rules are appropriately narrow or overly broad, and whether they properly distinguish personal survivor status from active advocacy. Note legal backing cited: a judge agreed Post removed Sonmez to uphold an image of unbiased news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of social-media discipline and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: How proportionate and appropriate disciplinary measures are for social-media missteps (e.g., paid administrative leave, month-long unpaid suspension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prior history, pattern of behavior, transparency of process, and whether discipline matches similar past cases. Example: Weigel's month suspension and Sonmez's 2020 paid leave are compared; one staffer suggested Weigel's 'questionable history' factored into the lengthier punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment about what constitutes 'poor judgment' online
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative judgment about tweets/retweets that 'undermine the work of colleagues' or display 'poor judgment' (Marty Baron said Sonmez 'displayed poor judgment' in 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify definitions of 'poor judgment' in policy and provide examples; weigh intent vs impact. Examples in the article: retweet of a sexist/homophobic tweet by Weigel; Sonmez linking to 2016 article about Kobe Bryant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for internal resolution versus public airing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether staff should raise complaints internally (Slack/editors) rather than publicly on Twitter; several colleagues said Sonmez should have taken complaints to editors and stayed off Twitter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether policies encourage internal reporting channels, protect complainants from retaliation, and define when public disclosure is justified. The article notes Sonmez first complained in a Slack channel then tweeted minutes later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collegiality and respectful workplace conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that employees 'treat each other with respect and kindness both in the newsroom and online' and policy emphasis on collegiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how policies and memos enforce collegiality, and whether calls for civility are balanced against allowing employees to raise legitimate grievances. Executive editor memo cited: 'We do not tolerate colleagues attacking colleagues either face to face or online.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable and even-handed enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether rules are applied equitably across staff (the guild described the Post's policies as 'not sufficiently equitable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for inconsistent outcomes (e.g., Montgomery received a verbal warning for a deleted tweet while others faced harsher penalties) and whether enforcement appears influenced by rank, relationships, or public pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and communication from leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: How clearly leadership communicates decisions and rationale to staff and the public (multiple memos, some brief and some stern; limited public comment beyond company statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether memos explain reasoning and next steps (e.g., pledge to update policy), and whether lack of public explanation fuels internal/external speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on sourcing relationships and institutional credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether internal controversies harm relationships with sources and the newsroom's ability to report (a source said 'sources have told them that they are hesitant to talk to the Post right now').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider empirical effects on sourcing, trust, and the dominant public narrative (e.g., how a newsroom's reputation can be overshadowed by internal drama even while covering major public stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between protecting complainants and preventing harassment/retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Need to protect employees who call out problems while preventing 'rallying the internet' to harass colleagues (Del Real accused Sonmez of 'repeated and targeted public harassment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate safeguards for complainants, anti-retaliation measures, and rules about public campaigning or mobilizing online attacks on coworkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of past history in disciplinary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an individual's past conduct is considered in current discipline (Weigel believed to have 'questionable history' and reportedly suspended once before).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that prior incidents are documented, considered consistently, and that any escalation of penalties follows a transparent policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and consistency of policy updates and follow-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether leadership follows through on internal recommendations and updates (internal 2020 report commissioned but two years later 'nothing has changed'), and executive pledge to update social media policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess processes for reviewing policy after incidents, whether union input is incorporated, and timelines for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership's ability to manage reputational fallout
rubrics_metrics.description: How effectively leaders contain or mitigate a controversy's external narrative (staffers' public defenses, questions about contrived messaging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether leadership's actions reduce harm and restore confidence or exacerbate perceptions of a toxic workplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standards and potential litigation implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding how legal rulings interact with newsroom policy (Sonmez's lawsuit alleged discrimination and retaliation; it was dismissed because no 'discriminatory motive' was shown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate legal precedents when designing policies; ensure actions can be legally justified and documented to withstand potential litigation.
